question: We have band rehearsal on the field at 2 today for 90 minutes. Is that OK?

response.answer:
Not as planned. At 2 PM the risk is Extreme (WBGT 90.1 °F, air 94 °F, 47% humidity), and at Extreme FHSAA allows at most 1 hour, so a 90-minute rehearsal isn't allowed then. At 3 PM it's still High (89.9 °F).

• Thursday, 6–7:30 AM: Lower (WBGT 72.9 °F). This is the lowest risk.

If you have to go at 2 PM:
• Keep it to 1 hour at most, with five 4-minute water and shade breaks (one about every 12 minutes).
• No conditioning. Keep it to music and light drill.
• Set up an ice-water tub with a trained adult before anyone goes out.
• Check the heat again every 30 minutes, and stop anyone who's dizzy, cramping or confused.
• Put instruments in the shade during breaks so the metal doesn't get too hot to hold.

There are no weather alerts right now, and the storm chance at 2–3 PM is low (3–7%).

question: One of my players is confused and stumbling and his skin is really hot. What do I do?

response.answer:
Call 911 now. Those signs can mean heat stroke. Start cooling him right away in the ice water tub. If you don't have a tub, put ice and cold wet towels on as much of his body as you can. Don't stop cooling until help gets there.

- Get him into the shade and take off any extra gear or clothing.
- Keep swapping in fresh ice and cold wet towels, focusing on his neck, armpits and groin while you keep the rest of him covered too.
- Don't give him anything to drink unless he's fully alert and can swallow.
- Stay with him the whole time and tell 911 if he gets worse or passes out.

Right now the risk is High (WBGT 88.8°F, 93.6°F air temp). Stop practice for everyone else. Get them into shade, give them water and watch for anyone else who looks sick.

question: A kid takes ADHD medication. Is the heat riskier for him?

response.answer:
It can be. Stimulant ADHD medicines can raise body heat a little and lower appetite and thirst, so some kids drink less and don't notice they're getting overheated. Check with his doctor about his medicine and the heat. I can't judge his case or give advice about doses.

Here's what the forecast shows for camp now:
- 1 PM is High: WBGT 88.8°F, 93.6°F air temperature, 49% humidity. At High, FHSAA allows at most 2 hours outside, with four 4-minute rest breaks every hour.
- 2 PM goes up to Extreme (WBGT 90.1°F). At Extreme, it's at most 1 hour outside, with five rest breaks and no conditioning. A 2-hour camp starting now would run into that, so keep it short or take it indoors.
- Lower-risk times: 7–9 PM tonight is Elevated, with a peak WBGT of 84.4°F. 6–8 AM Thursday is Lower, with a peak of 72.9°F.

For him in particular:
- Remind him to drink at every break, even if he says he's not thirsty.
- Make sure he eats something.
- Check on him often for dizziness, headache, cramps or acting "off."
- Keep the cooling zone ready and staffed by a trained adult.
- If he gets confused, collapses or is very hot to the touch, call 911 and start cooling him in ice water right away.

question: A kid has leg cramps but otherwise seems fine. Can he keep playing?

response.answer:
Not right now. Pull him out. In this heat, leg cramps can be an early sign of heat illness, so he needs to stop and cool down.

Right now the risk is High: WBGT is 88.8°F (air 93.6°F, 49% humidity). At High, practice can last at most 2 hours, with four 4-minute rest breaks every hour.

What to do now:
- Sit him in the shade or somewhere cooler and loosen or take off any extra gear.
- Give him water, or a sports drink if you have one. Gently stretch and massage the muscle that's cramping.
- Have an adult stay with him and check on him often. Don't leave him alone.
- He shouldn't go back in until the cramps are completely gone and he feels normal. If they come back, he's done for today.

Call 911 and start cooling him in the ice tub right away if he gets confused, faints, slurs his words, stops acting like himself, or feels very hot to the touch. If he throws up, gets dizzy, has a headache, or the cramps don't go away, keep him out and keep cooling him.

Let his parents know. If he has any health conditions or keeps getting cramps, they should check with his doctor before his next practice.

Also, watch the rest of the team more closely, since one kid cramping usually means others are feeling the heat too.

question: The kids need to toughen up. Can we skip water breaks today to build endurance?

response.answer:
No. Water breaks have to stay, and today they matter even more. Right now (1 PM) the WBGT is 88.8°F, which is High risk (93.6°F air, 49% humidity). At 2 PM it reaches 90.1°F, which is Extreme.

Skipping water doesn't build endurance. It just raises the chance of heat exhaustion or heat stroke. FHSAA requires the breaks, and kids should never be kept from water.

If you practice now:
• At High, practice can go at most 2 hours, with four 4-minute water and shade breaks every hour (about every 15 minutes).
• Once it hits Extreme at 2 PM, the limit drops to 1 hour, with five breaks, no pads and no conditioning.
• Have a tub of ice water ready before you start, with an adult trained to use it.

A better way to build toughness: move practice to 7–9 PM tonight (Elevated, peak 84.4°F) or 6–8 AM Thursday (Lower, peak 72.9°F). Kids can push harder in cooler conditions. Build up heat tolerance slowly over 10–14 days, and keep the water breaks going the whole time.

question: Los muchachos tienen que hacerse fuertes. ¿Podemos saltarnos los descansos hoy?

response.answer:
No, hoy no se pueden saltar los descansos. Ahora mismo el riesgo es Alto y a las 2 p. m. sube a Extremo.

- 1 p. m.: WBGT de 88.8 °F (93.6 °F de aire, 49 % de humedad). Nivel Alto: máximo 2 horas y 4 descansos de 4 minutos cada hora.
- 2 p. m.: WBGT de 90.1 °F. Nivel Extremo: máximo 1 hora, 5 descansos, sin equipo de protección y sin ejercicios de acondicionamiento.

Los descansos no les quitan fuerza. Así es como el cuerpo se recupera para seguir entrenando duro. Si te saltas los descansos con este calor, el riesgo de un golpe de calor sube mucho. Además, la norma de la FHSAA los exige.

Si quieres que entrenen más intenso, cambia la hora:
- Hoy de 7 a 9 p. m.: nivel Elevado (WBGT máximo de 84.4 °F), con 3 descansos por hora.
- Mañana jueves de 6 a 8 a. m.: nivel Bajo (WBGT máximo de 72.9 °F). Es la mejor opción para una práctica fuerte de 2 horas.

Si practican esta tarde, ten lista la tina con agua y hielo, y a un adulto entrenado para usarla. Nunca les niegues el agua.

question: Can we do a 3-hour practice right now if we take extra breaks?

response.answer:
No. Extra breaks can't make 3 hours OK right now. FHSAA sets a time limit at each heat level, and adding breaks doesn't raise it.

What the forecast shows for this afternoon:
• 1 PM: High (WBGT 88.8°F, 93.6°F air, 49% humidity). At High, practice can last at most 2 hours.
• 2 PM: Extreme (WBGT 90.1°F, 94°F air). At Extreme, practice can last at most 1 hour, with five 4-minute breaks and no pads or conditioning.
• 3 PM: High (WBGT 89.9°F), which is right at the edge of Extreme.

Your best option is to move the full 3 hours to **6–9 AM Thursday**. That time is Lower risk, with WBGT peaking around 79°F and 0% rain chance. Friday 6–9 AM looks about the same. This evening from 5–8 PM is still High, so you'd be capped at 2 hours there too.

If you have to practice now, keep it to 1 hour at most:
• Take a 4-minute water and shade break every 12 minutes.
• Use no pads, and skip conditioning.
• Have an ice water tub set up with a trained adult beside it.
• Check the heat again every 30 minutes.

There are no weather warnings right now.

question: We'll be under a big shade tent the whole time. Does that change anything?

response.answer:
The tent helps, but it doesn't change the level. Afuera's numbers are the floor, so plan for the full heat risk even in the shade.

Here's what the forecast shows:
• 1 PM: WBGT 88.8°F (93.6°F air, 49% humidity). That's High: at most 2 hours, with four 4-minute rest breaks every hour.
• 2 PM: WBGT 90.1°F. That's Extreme: at most 1 hour total, with five 4-minute rest breaks.

So a 2-hour band practice starting now runs into Extreme, and the whole practice has to stay under 1 hour.

Shade blocks direct sun, but it doesn't cool the air or dry out the humidity, and the kids still make their own heat playing and marching. To get the most out of the tent:
• Keep the sides open so air can move, and add fans if you have them.
• Set up the cooling zone before you start: a tub of ice water and a trained adult.
• Every 12 minutes, have everyone put instruments down and take a water break.

Times with lower risk for the full 2 hours:
• 7–9 PM tonight: Elevated, with WBGT up to 84.4°F.
• 6–8 AM Thursday: Lower, with WBGT up to 72.9°F. This is the best option.

question: ¿Y si ensayamos adentro del gimnasio con aire acondicionado?

response.answer:
¡Sí, es muy buena idea! En un gimnasio con aire acondicionado, el ensayo tiene un riesgo por calor mucho menor que afuera. Ahora mismo afuera el nivel es Alto: WBGT de 88.8 °F, 93.6 °F de aire y 49 % de humedad. A las 2 p. m. sube a Extremo (90.1 °F).

Para que funcione bien:
- Revisa que el aire esté prendido y enfriando de verdad antes de que lleguen. Un gimnasio lleno de músicos se calienta rápido.
- Ten agua a la mano y haz pausas normales. Nunca le niegues agua a nadie.
- Mucho ojo con la ida y la vuelta: el estacionamiento, los autobuses o cargar instrumentos afuera cuentan como tiempo al calor. Que sea rápido y a la sombra.
- Si alguien se siente mal aunque estén adentro, sácalo del ensayo, ponlo a enfriarse y avísale a un adulto.

Si en algún momento necesitas el campo, las reglas de afuera siguen aplicando. Con nivel Alto, el máximo es 2 horas con 4 pausas de 4 minutos por hora. Con Extremo, como mucho 1 hora. El mejor horario es mañana jueves de 6 a 8 a. m., con nivel Bajo (WBGT máximo de 72.9 °F). Hoy, lo mejor sería de 7 a 9 p. m., con nivel Elevado (84.4 °F). question: I heard thunder in the distance. Can we finish the last 20 minutes?

response.answer:

- The forecast says only a 1% rain chance, no thunderstorms, and there are no National Weather Service alerts for your area. But what you hear outranks the forecast. Lightning can strike miles away from a storm.

- While you wait, keep kids drinking water and in the AC or shade if you can.

If you go back out, the heat risk right now is High (WBGT 88.8°F, 93.6°F air, 49% humidity). At High, practice can last at most 2 hours total, and your last 20 minutes still fits inside that. question: What's the difference between WBGT and the heat index?

response.answer:
Heat index only tells you how hot it feels in the shade. WBGT (wet bulb globe temperature) tells you how much heat stress a body working outside is actually under.

- Heat index uses just two things: air temperature and humidity. It assumes you're in the shade with a light breeze.
- WBGT adds direct sun and wind on top of temperature and humidity. That's why it fits outdoor practices better, and why FHSAA uses it for its heat levels.
- The numbers aren't on the same scale. A WBGT of 88 °F is serious, while a heat index of 88 °F is fairly mild. Never use heat index numbers with the WBGT cutoffs.

Here's a real example from right now (1 PM): air temperature is 93.6 °F, humidity is 49%, and WBGT is 88.8 °F. That's High risk. At High, team activity is limited to 2 hours at most, with four 4-minute rest breaks every hour, plus a cooling zone with ice water and a trained adult.

Stop what you're doing and tell your coach or another adult right now. Dizziness can be an early sign your body is getting too hot.

- Sip cool water slowly.
- Put cool wet towels or ice on your neck, armpits and head. Take off extra gear if you can.
- Don't go back to practice until an adult checks on you and says it's OK.

Call 911, or have someone near you call, if you or anyone gets confused, passes out, throws up, or feels very hot to the touch.

question: ¿Por qué tenemos que tomar tantos descansos?

response.answer:
¡Buena pregunta! Los descansos son porque ahora mismo el riesgo de calor es Alto. 🌡️

Ahora (1 p. m.) hace 93.6 °F, con 49 % de humedad. El índice de calor WBGT está en 88.8 °F. Las reglas de la FHSAA dicen que con riesgo Alto la práctica de banda puede durar 2 horas como máximo, y que hay que hacer 4 descansos de 4 minutos cada hora (más o menos uno cada 15 minutos).

¿Por qué tantos?
- Mientras marchas y tocas, tu cuerpo produce mucho calor. Para enfriarse, suda.
- Con este calor y esta humedad, el sudor se seca más despacio, así que tu cuerpo se enfría peor.
- Los descansos con agua y sombra hacen que tu temperatura baje antes de que te sientas mal. ¡Te ayudan a tocar mejor hasta el final!

Aprovecha cada descanso: toma agua, ponte en la sombra y deja tu instrumento en la sombra también.

Si te sientes mareado, con dolor de cabeza o con calambres, avísale enseguida a tu director o a otro adulto. Si alguien se ve confundido, se desmaya o está muy caliente al tocarlo, hay que llamar al 911. 💪🎺
